sources.title: The Origin and Evolution of Cells
sources.publisher: Sinauer Associates; hosted by NCBI Bookshelf
sources.version: The Cell: A Molecular Approach, 2nd edition; NCBI Bookshelf ID NBK9841
sources.locator: Sections Present-Day Prokaryotes and Eukaryotic Cells. Bacteria are 1 to 10 micrometres across with 0.6 to 5 million base pairs of DNA; Escherichia coli is a rod about 1 micrometre in diameter and 2 micrometres long, with a rigid cell wall outside its plasma membrane, one circular DNA molecule in the nucleoid which, unlike a nucleus, is not membrane-separated from the cytoplasm, and about 30,000 ribosomes. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus, linear DNA, and frequently a thousandfold the volume.
sources.license: Copyright 2000 Geoffrey M Cooper; facts-only use, with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the structural criterion separating the two cell classes, the dimensions and contents of a typical prokaryotic cell, the range of bacterial genome sizes, and the order-of-magnitude volume difference between the two cell types. No wording, figure, table, or example was copied or adapted. The cylinder and sphere models, every calculation built on those dimensions, and all teaching tasks are this lesson's own work.

sources.title: Transcription-translation coupling: Recent advances and future perspectives
sources.locator: Introduction: unlike eukaryotes, where transcription and translation are separated by a nuclear envelope, in bacterial cells the two processes occur within the same compartment, and a pioneering ribosome starts translation on nascent messenger RNA that is still being actively transcribed by RNA polymerase.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that a nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation in eukaryotes while the two share one compartment in bacteria, and that a bacterial ribosome can translate a transcript that is still being made.
